query: For refractory materials, experiments at the solid-to-fluid transition are difficult and yield sparse, scattered data, while the large compositional space of high-entropy systems makes systematic screening impractical. DFT free-energy studies can determine the transition from the crossing of solid and dense-fluid Gibbs energies and provide associated thermodynamic properties, but their reliance on extensive ab initio molecular dynamics makes them costly. TOR-TILD has shown high efficiency for elemental and binary systems, yet becomes substantially slower for multicomponent systems. Any broadly useful approach must retain ab initio-level accuracy, represent all thermodynamic effects identified as important, treat both phases around the transition, and remain practical across relevant compositions and temperatures. For a multicomponent high-entropy material in these high-temperature states, what single intervention could improve determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and causal mechanism, its predicted outcome relative to existing experimental and computational baselines, its boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive experiment or benchmark that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Intervention with high-entropy alloy design using configurational entropy to stabilize a single-phase solid solution can improve determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity in multicomponent high-entropy materials.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy material in a solid state
generation.intervention: Design of high-entropy alloy using configurational entropy to stabilize a single-phase solid solution
generation.mechanism: Entropy-driven thermodynamic stabilization, kinetic stabilization, and sluggish diffusion prevent phase separation and elemental segregation, enabling the formation of uniform alloy structures from immiscible elements.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity
generation.baseline: Existing experimental and computational methods for determining thermodynamic properties of high-entropy materials
generation.boundary: High-temperature states, solid-to-fluid transition, multicomponent high-entropy materials
generation.uncertainty: Insufficient data on the effects of configurational entropy on thermodynamic properties of high-entropy materials, limitations of computational models and experimental methods

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature experiments on multicomponent high-entropy materials with varying levels of configurational entropy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention with high-entropy alloy design using configurational entropy does not improve the determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: Equimolar quinary alloys from 40 elements (e.g., AlCoMnNiV, CoFeMnNiZn, Cantor alloy CoCrFeMnNi). Question: How can multi-elemental alloy nanoparticles (MEA-NPs) composed of traditionally immiscible elements be rationally designed and rapidly synthesized to achieve high catalytic efficiency and durability for ammonia decomposition?. System: RuRhCoNi (Ru-4 MEA-NPs) and RuRhCoNiIr (Ru-5 MEA-NPs) nanoparticles; precursor elements: Ru, Rh, Co, Ni, Ir, Pd, Cr, Fe, Cu, Mo. Processing: Rapid high-temperature synthesis via electrical Joule heating: multi-elemental salt precursors (0.05 M in ethanol) deposited on activated carbon nanofibers, heated to 1500 K for 500 ms (0.5 s), followed by quenching.
